title: Fazola, Sal Franzella and New Orleans clarinetists
summary: Reed preferences of Fazola, comparison with Sal Franzella, a Mardi Gras parade band and Raymond Burke at the Plantation Club.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Who were the great clarinetists? Favorites and rivals

blocks.x: Well, I have a few little questions. I'd be glad if you would. Okay. Uh, we covered a lot of territory. Uh, what kind of reeds did Fahs use? You were talking about something? Vandora.

He liked them. He liked them. He, uh, he much preferred the Vandora reeds than anything else. And, uh, when he didn't have, uh, money to buy a box, well, I would pick out the very best reeds in the box for him. And, uh, at that time, uh, Fahs and Sal Franzella were very close. Well, I say friends. They were, uh, Fahs was a great, great jazz musician. And, uh, Sal Franzella was, uh, historically a tremendously well-trained saxophonist in China. He later played with Paul Whiteman. And, uh, New Orleans is full of great stories about, uh, himself. About, uh, uh... Fahsolo? No, not Fahsolo. Uh, this, uh, uh... Well, anyway, he later became a salesman with the Salman Company. He was a former white man. He died in New Orleans a few years ago. He later became a very fine jazz pianist, too, but not. See, there's such a difference in players. Uh-huh. I mean, he could do anything with a horn. Yet, Fahsolo was a much better jazz man. You know, for one thing, the tone was so different. The tone is entirely different, it's true. I don't know if you remember this, but, uh, Fahsolo played the album system, and there is a little tonal difference in the two. Yeah.

Yeah. I got to know, well, there were so many good clients in New Orleans during the time I was down there digging. I once marched in a parade. The only parade I ever marched was in the evening, during the Marley Grove, in New Orleans. The same Johnny Brent got me the job, and they had, in this band, they had Azola, they had Nina Pekona, they had Myer Weinberg, who was Gene Meyer, I think he calls himself now. They just had all of the jazz musicians in this parade, and some guys that maybe didn't play very often at all, but they'd pull them out of the Union with getting at least enough to play the Union dues for the year, you know, make it on a parade. But New Orleans was, I tell you, I really enjoyed it, and I learned so much. I got, I'm not a real good friend of Raymond Burke at all. I just know him. But he was playing at the, and I'll take it back, there was another club in the quarter, it was called the Plantation Club. And Ray, Ray Burke was playing there, in 1932. And they had a little Port East Band. And it was, it was quite good. They wanted radio every night. Well, there were just so many good New Orleans musicians, like Bill Pedrona, who you never heard of, but one of the band, great trumpet players. And, excuse me, go ahead.
